docs.title: Matrix and Vectors
docs.text:
To understand machine learning in-depth, let us first understand a few topics related to linear algebra. You do not necessarily need to understand linear algebra in-depth, to get started with machine learning. However, it will be useful in understanding the mathematics behind machine learning algorithms.

In linear algebra, data is mostly represented using matrices and vectors.

docs.title: Matrix
docs.text: Matrices (plural of matrix) are used throughout machine learning algorithms, specifically for input variables, i.e., the variables we try to understand in machine learning. A matrix of size LaTeX: m\times n is a two-dimensional array that has m rows and n columns.

docs.title: Vector
docs.text:
A vector is a one-dimensional array that has only one row - called a row vector, or just one column, also called a column vector.

For example, in the below figure, X is a matrix with 3 rows and 2 columns, while Y is a simple column vector.

docs.title: Key Equations (MathJax)
docs.text:
• Projection of a vector \( \mathbf{x} \) onto unit vector \( \mathbf{u} \): \[ \mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; (\mathbf{x}!\cdot!\mathbf{u})\,\mathbf{u} \]

  • Least‑squares solution (full column rank): \[ \hat{\mathbf{w}} \;=\; (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top \mathbf{y} \]

docs.title: Visual (inline SVG – projection)
docs.text: u (unit) x proj_u(x)

docs.title: Real‑Time Use Case
docs.text: Latency‑sensitive vector search: Project high‑dimensional query embeddings onto a smaller subspace (e.g., PCs) to reduce ANN query time while retaining most energy.

docs.title: Python Snippet
docs.text:
import numpy as np

# Query and basis (orthonormal columns)
x = np.random.randn(768)
U = np.linalg.qr(np.random.randn(768, 64))[0]   # 64-dim subspace
proj = U @ (U.T @ x)     # projection
residual = x - proj
energy_kept = np.linalg.norm(proj)**2 / np.linalg.norm(x)**2
print(f"Energy kept: {energy_kept:.3f}")

Back to Top

docs.title: Eigenvectors & Eigenvalues
docs.text: Eigenvectors keep their direction under a linear map \(A\): \( A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v} \). Non‑trivial solutions exist where \( \det(A-\lambda I)=0 \).

docs.title: Visual (shear eigenvector intuition)
docs.text: v Av = λv

docs.title: Real‑Time Use Case
docs.text: RNN stability & spectral norm: Ensure the largest \(|\lambda|\) of the recurrent matrix is \(<1\) to prevent exploding activations. Also used for spectral clustering and PageRank (dominant eigenvector).

docs.title: Python Snippet
docs.text:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[0.9, 0.2],
              [0.1, 0.8]])
eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
spectral_radius = np.max(np.abs(eigvals))
print("Eigenvalues:", eigvals)
print("Spectral radius:", spectral_radius)

docs.title: Why are Eigenvectors important?
docs.text:
The directional invariance of Eigenvectors turns out to be an incredibly important mathematical property, and is utilized by many applications - Principal Component Analysis (PCA), for example, is a highly popular data projection technique that can be used to reduce the dimensionality of a dataset and visualize it in lower dimensions.

Back to Top

docs.title: Variance:
docs.text: Variance helps us understand how far our random variable is spread out from the mean, for example, the income of the people may have a high variance as some people may have high income levels.

docs.title: Covariance
docs.text:
Covariance measures joint variability.

It measures how much two random variables vary together. e.g. The income of a person and the expenses of that person in a population. More precisely, covariance refers to the measure of how two random variables in a data set will change together. A positive covariance means that the two variables at hand are positively related, and they move in the same direction. A negative covariance means that the variables are inversely related, or that they move in opposite directions.

For data matrix \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) (rows = samples), the unbiased covariance is: \[ \Sigma \;=\; \frac{1}{n-1}(X-\bar{X})^\top(X-\bar{X}) \]

docs.title: Real‑Time Use Case
docs.text: Drift monitoring: Recompute feature covariance online and compare with a baseline to detect distribution shift in production.

docs.title: Python Snippet
docs.text:
import numpy as np

X_ref = np.random.randn(10_000, 16)            # baseline
X_now = np.random.randn(10_000, 16) + 0.2      # shifted

def cov(x):
    x = x - x.mean(0, keepdims=True)
    return (x.T @ x) / (x.shape[0]-1)

Sigma_ref = cov(X_ref)
Sigma_now = cov(X_now)

fro_diff = np.linalg.norm(Sigma_ref - Sigma_now, 'fro')
print("Frobenius difference:", fro_diff)

Back to Top

docs.title: Kullback-Leibler KL Divergence
docs.text: For continuous densities \(p,q\): \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\parallel q)=\int p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}dx\). For Gaussians \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)\) and \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_0,\Sigma_0)\): \[ D_{\mathrm{KL}} = \tfrac{1}{2}!\left(\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_0^{-1}\Sigma) + (\mu_0-\mu)^\top\Sigma_0^{-1}(\mu_0-\mu) - k + \ln\frac{\det\Sigma_0}{\det\Sigma}\right) \]

docs.title: Visual
docs.text: p(x) q(x)

docs.title: Real‑Time Use Case
docs.text: Anomaly scoring in streams: Fit \(q\) to recent data; score new batches with \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\parallel q)\) using a reference \(p\).

docs.title: Python Snippet
docs.text:
import numpy as np

mu_p = np.zeros(8);  Sigma_p = np.eye(8)
mu_q = np.ones(8)*0.3;  Sigma_q = np.eye(8)*1.2

def kl_gaussians(mu, Sigma, mu0, Sigma0):
    k = mu.shape[0]
    iS0 = np.linalg.inv(Sigma0)
    term1 = np.trace(iS0 @ Sigma)
    term2 = (mu0 - mu).T @ iS0 @ (mu0 - mu)
    term3 = -k
    term4 = np.log(np.linalg.det(Sigma0)/np.linalg.det(Sigma))
    return 0.5*(term1 + term2 + term3 + term4)

print("KL(p||q) ≈", kl_gaussians(mu_p, Sigma_p, mu_q, Sigma_q))

docs.title: The intuition behind the KL divergence score:
docs.text:
When the probability for an event from p is large, but the probability for the same event in q is small, there is a large divergence. When the probability from p is small and the probability from q is large, there is also a large divergence, but not as large as in the former case.

Back to Top

docs.title: Unsupervised Learning
docs.text:
Discover structure without labels: clustering, density estimation, dimensionality reduction, topic modeling, etc.

Data science and machine learning algorithmic techniques can be divided into three categories:

  • Supervised Learning: The algorithm has prior data (labeled data) to learn from.
  • Unsupervised Learning: The algorithm has no prior labeled data to learn from — it learns from unlabeled data by finding patterns among examples and grouping them accordingly.
  • Reinforcement Learning: The algorithm learns patterns or behaviors recursively by taking actions to maximize a certain reward, and uses feedback from the environment to learn the best action to take under the right circumstances.

docs.title: What is Unsupervised Learning?
docs.text:
Unsupervised Learning is a category of techniques that train computers to use a set of unlabeled / unseen data and learn by themselves. The algorithm is provided with a large volume of data and expected to identify hidden patterns.

  • Since there's no prior label available for each data instance, there is no defined correct outcome.
  • The machine’s task is to determine whether there are patterns in the given data.

docs.title: Clustering
docs.text:
Clustering divides data into groups such that:

  • Each group shares similar properties internally
  • Each group is dissimilar to other groups

docs.title: Example: Customer Segmentation
docs.text:
A company launching a new product wants to segment customers to target the right audience. Possible segmentation criteria:

  1. Demographics: Occupation, age, gender
  2. Income & Spending Habits
  3. Geographic Location

This is unsupervised learning because:

  • There was no labeled information about customers
  • Features such as age, gender, income were used
  • The algorithm grouped similar individuals together without knowing the meaning of each group

docs.title: Association
docs.text:
Association learning is a rule-based machine learning and data mining technique.

  • Finds important relationships between variables or features in a dataset
  • Checks for dependency of one data item on another
  • Often used to increase profitability via cross-selling or recommendations

Example: If customers who buy bread often also buy butter, the store can place these items together to increase sales.

docs.title: Visual (concept map)
docs.text: Clustering Density Topics Dim. Reduction

docs.title: Real‑Time Use Case
docs.text: User segmentation: Cluster users nightly to personalize recommendations and pricing.

docs.title: Python Snippet
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

X = np.random.randn(50_000, 16)  # features
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=8, n_init='auto', random_state=0).fit(X)
labels = kmeans.labels_
print("Cluster sizes:", np.bincount(labels))

Back to Top

docs.title: Dimensionality Reduction
docs.text:
Dimensionality reduction is the transformation of data from a high-dimensional space into a low-dimensional space such that:

  • The low-dimensional representation retains meaningful properties of the original data
  • The structure is close to its intrinsic dimension

Common methods:

  • PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
  • t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding)

  • UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection)

  • PCA: projects onto directions of maximal variance (eigenvectors of covariance).

The main idea of principal component analysis (PCA) is to reduce the dimensionality of a dataset consisting of many variables correlated with each other, either heavily or lightly, while retaining the variation present in the dataset.

This is done by transforming the variables to a new coordinate space of variables, which are known as principal components (or simply, the PCs), and are orthogonal to each other.

The selection of principal components is such that the retention of variation present in the original variables is the maximum for the first principal component and decreases as we move down in order. The principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and hence they are orthogonal.

\[ X \approx ZW^\top,\quad W = \text{top-}k\ \text{eigenvectors of } \Sigma \]

docs.title: Visual (principal axes)
docs.text: PC1 PC2

docs.title: Real‑Time Use Case
docs.text: Telemetry compression: Stream PCA to keep top‑k components for downstream anomaly detection and faster query.

docs.title: Python Snippet - Two Dimensions
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

X = np.random.randn(10000, 256)
pca = PCA(n_components=32, svd_solver='randomized', random_state=0).fit(X)
Z = pca.transform(X)
print("Explained variance ratio sum:", pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum())

docs.title: Python Snippet - Three Dimensions
docs.text:
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(1)

vec1 = np.array([0, 0, 0])
mat1 = np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]])
sample_for_class1 = np.random.multivariate_normal(vec1, mat1, 20).T
assert sample_for_class1.shape == (3, 20), "The dimension of the sample_for_class1 matrix is not 3x20"

vec2 = np.array([1, 1, 1])
mat2 = np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]])
sample_for_class2 = np.random.multivariate_normal(vec2, mat2, 20).T
assert sample_for_class2.shape == (3, 20), "The dimension of the sample_for_class2 matrix is not 3x20"

all_data = np.concatenate((sample_for_class1, sample_for_class2), axis=1)
assert all_data.shape == (3, 40), "The dimension of the all_data matrix is not 3x20"
  • t‑SNE/UMAP: preserve local neighborhood structure for visualization.

The t-SNE algorithm calculates a similarity measure between pairs of instances in the high dimensional space and in the low dimensional space. This is done by setting the probabilities from the low-dimensional space similar to those of the high-dimensional space. We measure the difference between the probability distributions of the two-dimensional spaces using Kullback-Leibler divergence and try to optimize it.

Back to Top

docs.title: Distance & Scaling Measures
docs.text:
Unsupervised learning algorithms use different distance measures or similarity/dissimilarity measures between each pair of observations to group data into different clusters. Points which are close to each other on that distance metric are likely to be grouped into the same cluster, while points far apart on that distance metric are likely to be members of different clusters. All this is done by computing a distance matrix that has distances between every pair of observations. There are different ways of calculating these distances, some of which are mentioned below:

Euclidean distance: Euclidean distance is calculated as the square root of the sum of the squared differences between two vectors.

  • L1 (Manhattan): \( |\mathbf{x}|_1 = \sum_i |x_i| \)
  • L2 (Euclidean): \( |\mathbf{x}|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_i x_i^2} \)
  • Cosine distance: \( 1 - \frac{\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}}{|\mathbf{x}|_2|\mathbf{y}|_2} \)

docs.title: Real‑Time Use Case
docs.text: Vector search: Use cosine similarity for text/image embeddings; standardize vectors to unit norm for stable nearest‑neighbor ranking.

docs.title: Python Snippet
docs.text:
import numpy as np

X = np.random.randn(1000, 768)
X = X / np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1, keepdims=True)  # unit-norm
q = np.random.randn(768); q /= np.linalg.norm(q)
scores = X @ q
ix = np.argsort(-scores)[:5]
print("Top-5 indices:", ix)

docs.title: Why Scaling is Important
docs.text:
Input variables in a dataset may have different units (e.g., kilometers, hours, kilograms), resulting in different scales. Without scaling: - 1 km would be treated the same as 1 kg or 1 hour. - Features with larger numeric ranges may dominate the model’s decision-making. - Models become unstable and biased towards features with higher values.

Scaling ensures all features contribute equally to the model, preventing one variable from overpowering others due to its numerical magnitude.

docs.title: 1. Normalization (Min–Max Scaling)
docs.text:
Transforms all values to a 0–1 range.

Formula:

\[ y \;=\; \frac{x - \mathrm{min}}{\mathrm{max} - \mathrm{min}} \]

Where: - \( y \) → normalized value - \( x \) → original value - \( \mathrm{min} \) → minimum value of \( x \) in dataset - \( \mathrm{max} \) → maximum value of \( x \) in dataset

docs.title: 2. Standardization (Z-score Scaling)
docs.text:
Centers the data so the mean = 0 and standard deviation = 1.

Formula:

\[ y \;=\; \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} \]

Where: - \( y \) → standardized value - \( x \) → original value - \( \mu \) → mean of \( x \) - \( \sigma \) → standard deviation of \( x \)

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Normalization → Good for distance-based algorithms like \( k \)-NN, K-Means, Neural Networks.
  • Standardization → Good when algorithms assume normally-distributed data (Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, SVM).

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Normalization: Best for algorithms relying on distances (KNN, K-Means) or neural networks.
  • Standardization: Best for algorithms assuming normality (linear regression, logistic regression, SVM).

Back to Top

docs.title: K‑means Clustering
docs.text:
Objective: minimize within‑cluster sum of squares. Lloyd’s algorithm alternates assignment and centroid update.

K-means Clustering is an unsupervised learning algorithm. Like other clustering algorithms, it tries to aggregate similar objects into groups called clusters. In K-means Clustering, K refers to the number of clusters required. The concept of a centroid, which is the geometric center of a cluster, is used to determine the clusters that K-means finds in the dataset.

Let’s understand this using an example. Suppose you go to a vegetable shop to buy some vegetables. There, you'll see different kinds of vegetables. One thing you may notice is that the vegetables will be arranged in a group of their type. The carrots and radishes will probably be kept together in one place, onion and garlic will probably be arranged in another place, potatoes will be kept together, and so on. This arrangement resembles a group or a cluster, where each vegetable is kept within its kind of group, forming the clusters.

docs.title: Real‑Time Use Case
docs.text: Customer micro‑segmentation updated hourly for marketing triggers and content personalization.

docs.title: Python Snippet
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

X = np.r_[np.random.randn(500,2)+np.array([0,0]),
          np.random.randn(500,2)+np.array([4,4])]
km = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init='auto', random_state=42).fit(X)
print("Centroids:\n", km.cluster_centers_)

docs.title: Example: K-means on 1D Data
docs.text:
Let’s understand K-means clustering with an example.

Given:

\[ N = { 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 11, 13, 15 } \]

All points lie on the x-axis.

docs.title: Step 2 — Initialize Centroids Randomly
docs.text:
\[ c_1 = 3, \quad c_2 = 12 \]

Since all points are on the x-axis (y = 0), the distance between two points is: \( d = |x_2 - x_1| \)

docs.title: Step 3.1 — Assign Points to Closest Centroid
docs.text:
Data Point Distance to \( c_1 = 3 \) Distance to \( c_2 = 12 \) Cluster Assigned 2 1 10 c₁ 3 0 9 c₁ 4 1 8 c₁ 5 2 7 c₁ 10 7 2 c₂ 11 8 1 c₂ 13 10 1 c₂ 15 12 3 c₂

Result after assignment:

\[ \text{Cluster } c_1: { 2, 3, 4, 5 } \] \[ \text{Cluster } c_2: { 10, 11, 13, 15 } \]

docs.title: Step 4 — Repeat Until Convergence
docs.text:
Repeat Step 3 (assignment and update) until there is no change in centroids.

docs.text: Graphs \(G=(V,E)\) represent relationships (users, items, web pages).

docs.title: Example Scenario: Email Classification — Spam vs. Not Spam
1. Supervised Learning
docs.text: In supervised learning, the algorithm is trained on labeled data.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: We have a dataset of past emails where each email is already labeled as "Spam" or "Not Spam".

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Training Data:
  2. Email text → "You won a prize!" → Spam
  3. Email text → "Meeting at 10am" → Not Spam
  4. Email text → "Claim your free gift" → Spam
  5. Features extracted (word counts, sender address, links, etc.).
  6. The model learns patterns that distinguish spam from non-spam.
  7. For a new incoming email, the model predicts:
  8. "Spam" if it matches spam-like patterns.
  9. "Not Spam" otherwise.

docs.title: Real-Time Example
docs.text: • Gmail uses supervised learning with millions of labeled spam/not spam examples from user feedback.

docs.title: Python (Supervised — Logistic Regression Example)
docs.text:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

# Training Data
emails = [
    "You won a prize",
    "Meeting at 10am",
    "Claim your free gift",
    "Project deadline extended"
]
labels = [1, 0, 1, 0]  # 1 = Spam, 0 = Not Spam

# Feature Extraction
vectorizer = CountVectorizer()
X = vectorizer.fit_transform(emails)

# Train Model
model = LogisticRegression()
model.fit(X, labels)

# Predict
test_email = ["Free tickets to the concert"]
print(model.predict(vectorizer.transform(test_email)))  # Output: [1] (Spam)

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 2. Unsupervised Learning
docs.text: In unsupervised learning, the algorithm works with unlabeled data.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: We have a large number of past emails but no spam/not spam labels.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The model groups emails into clusters based on content similarity.
  2. After clustering:
  3. Cluster A: "You won a prize", "Claim your free gift", "Free tickets" → Likely spam.
  4. Cluster B: "Meeting at 10am", "Project deadline extended" → Likely not spam.
  5. Labels are inferred later by human inspection or heuristics.

docs.title: Real-Time Example
docs.text: • Email filtering systems can first group unknown emails, then allow humans to label clusters, speeding up the training process.

docs.title: Python (Unsupervised — KMeans Example)
docs.text:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# Unlabeled Emails
emails = [
    "You won a prize",
    "Meeting at 10am",
    "Claim your free gift",
    "Project deadline extended"
]

# Feature Extraction
vectorizer = CountVectorizer()
X = vectorizer.fit_transform(emails)

# Apply KMeans
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=2, random_state=42)
kmeans.fit(X)

# Cluster Assignments
for email, label in zip(emails, kmeans.labels_):
    print(f"{email} → Cluster {label}")

↩ Back to Top

✅ Key Difference: - Supervised: Needs labeled data upfront. - Unsupervised: Finds patterns without labels.

docs.title: Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning — Example Scenarios
docs.text:
This document presents various real-world examples of Supervised and Unsupervised learning problems, including their key components: features, labels, and the reasoning for classification.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 1. Air Pollution Prediction
docs.text:
Scenario: You measured the concentration of a certain type of air pollutant at different locations, under various weather conditions, times of day, and days of the week. Now you want to predict the air pollution concentration at a new location without additional measurements.

Learning Type: Supervised Learning ✅

Reasoning: - Features: Location, weather conditions, day, and time. - Label: Air pollution concentration (numerical). - This is a regression problem because the label is a continuous numeric value (e.g., 2000 particles/cm³ is less than 6000 particles/cm³).

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 2. Social Group Discovery in Offices
docs.text:
Scenario: A researcher observed office workers over a month and recorded their interactions. The goal is to discover friendships or social groups.

Learning Type: Unsupervised Learning ✅

Reasoning: - Features: Records of interactions between people. - Labels: None (unknown social groups). - The goal is clustering people into groups based on interaction patterns.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 3. Rocket Booster Lift Prediction (NASA)
docs.text:
Scenario: NASA simulates rocket booster performance under various specifications. They want to predict simulated lift for new specifications without running full simulations.

Learning Type: Supervised Learning ✅

Reasoning: - Features: Rocket booster specifications. - Label: Simulated lift (numerical). - This is a regression task predicting a continuous variable.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 4. Bird Video Compression
docs.text:
Scenario: A small bird-monitoring camera captures video, but bandwidth is limited. The goal is to compress video before transmission.

Learning Type: Unsupervised Learning ✅

Reasoning: - Features: Pixel values over time. - Labels: None. - Uses clustering (e.g., grouping similar pixels in color and time) for compression.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 5. Student Algorithm Error Analysis
docs.text:
Scenario: In an online course, students implement an algorithm for an exercise. You want to understand the different types of errors to improve teaching.

Learning Type: Unsupervised Learning ✅

Reasoning: - Features: Student solutions and code errors. - Labels: None (no predefined error categories). - Goal is to find patterns in mistakes, possibly for adaptive learning.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 6. Email Classification (Spam or Not Spam)
docs.text:
Scenario: A dataset of emails, each labeled as spam or not spam. You want to predict whether a new email is spam.

Learning Type: Supervised Learning ✅

Reasoning: - Features: Words/phrases, metadata, and structure of the email. - Label: Spam or Not Spam (categorical). - This is a classification problem because the label is discrete with no inherent order.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: What is Clustering?
docs.text:
Clustering is an unsupervised learning task that groups data points into clusters so that points in the same cluster are similar to each other and dissimilar to points in other clusters. Unlike classification, clustering operates without labels, discovering structure directly from the data.

  • Goal: assign each data point to exactly one group (hard clustering) or to groups with probabilities (soft clustering).
  • Outcome: descriptive structure that can reveal segments, communities, or latent themes.

Back to Top

docs.title: Example: Archaeology Dig
docs.text: Imagine an archaeology site where each artifact’s location is recorded as (east, north) coordinates relative to a marker. Historians suspect three families lived at the site. By clustering the artifact locations, we may recover three spatial groups that correspond to where those families lived and discarded objects.

docs.title: Visual (inline SVG sketch)
docs.text:
Visual (inline SVG sketch) Family A Family B Family C

Back to Top

docs.title: Similarity & Distance
docs.text:
Clustering depends on a similarity notion. Common choices use a distance metric \( d(\cdot,\cdot) \) over feature vectors \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d\).

  • Euclidean: \( d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = \lVert \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y} \rVert_2 \)
  • Manhattan: \( d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = \lVert \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y} \rVert_1 \)
  • Cosine distance: \( d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = 1 - \frac{\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert} \)

Choose a distance aligned with the data geometry (e.g., cosine for text embeddings).

Back to Top

docs.title: Clustering vs. Classification
docs.text:
• Classification (supervised): learn a mapping from features to known labels (e.g., family names).
  • Clustering (unsupervised): discover groups with no labels available; the structure is inferred from the data alone.

Back to Top

docs.title: 🔵 K-means (hard, centroid-based)
docs.text:
Minimizes within-cluster variance (sum of squared distances to cluster centroids). Objective:

The K-means objective:

\[ \min_{\{C_k\}_{k=1}^K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{\mathbf{x}\in C_k} \bigl\| \mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k \bigr\|_2^2 \]
  • Fast and scalable; assumes roughly spherical clusters of similar size.
  • Sensitive to initialization and outliers.

docs.title: 🟢 Hierarchical clustering (agglomerative/divisive)
docs.text:
• Builds a tree (dendrogram) of nested clusters using a linkage: single, complete, average, Ward’s.
  • No need to pre-specify \(K\); choose a cut level on the dendrogram.

docs.title: 🟠 DBSCAN (density-based)
docs.text:
• Finds clusters as regions of high density separated by low-density regions.
  • Parameters: \(\varepsilon\) (neighborhood radius) and minPts.
  • Detects arbitrary shapes and flags noise; struggles with varying densities.

docs.title: 🟣 Gaussian Mixture Models (soft clustering)
docs.text:
• Probabilistic model: data from a mixture of Gaussians; assigns soft responsibilities.
  • Learned via EM algorithm; captures elliptical clusters with covariance structure.

Back to Top

docs.title: Choosing the Number of Clusters
docs.text:
• Elbow method: inspect the curve of within-cluster sum of squares vs. \(K\) and look for an “elbow.”
  • Silhouette analysis: prefer \(K\) that maximizes average silhouette score.
  • Domain constraints: business or scientific context may dictate plausible \(K\).

Back to Top

docs.title: Evaluating Cluster Quality
docs.text:
Given a point \(i\), let \(a(i)\) be the mean distance to points in its own cluster, and \(b(i)\) the smallest mean distance to points in another cluster. The silhouette is:

\[ s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max\{a(i), b(i)\}} \in [-1, 1]. \]

  • Average \(s(i)\) close to 1 ⇒ well-separated clusters; near 0 ⇒ overlapping; negative ⇒ misassigned.

Other diagnostics: Calinski–Harabasz, Davies–Bouldin, stability under resampling.

Back to Top

docs.title: Challenges & Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Scale sensitivity: standardize features; otherwise one feature may dominate distance.
  • Non-spherical structure: K-means may fail on elongated or manifold-shaped clusters.
  • Outliers & noise: can skew centroids; use robust methods (DBSCAN, trimming).
  • High dimensionality: distance concentration; consider PCA or UMAP first.
  • Initialization: multiple restarts (K-means++), consensus clustering for robustness.

Back to Top

docs.title: Minimal Python Example
docs.text:
# Minimal clustering demo: K-means and DBSCAN on 2D data
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, DBSCAN
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# synthetic data
X, y_true = make_blobs(n_samples=600, centers=3, cluster_std=0.75, random_state=42)

# K-means
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init="auto", random_state=42)
labels_km = kmeans.fit_predict(X)
sil_km = silhouette_score(X, labels_km)

# DBSCAN (tune eps/min_samples for data scale)
db = DBSCAN(eps=0.8, min_samples=5)
labels_db = db.fit_predict(X)
mask = labels_db != -1  # ignore noise for silhouette if needed
sil_db = silhouette_score(X[mask], labels_db[mask]) if mask.any() else float("nan")

print(f"K-means silhouette: {sil_km:.3f}")
print(f"DBSCAN silhouette (excl. noise): {sil_db:.3f}")

Back to Top

docs.title: K-Means Clustering
docs.text:
K-Means Clustering is one of the most popular algorithms in Unsupervised Learning.

Why K-Means is popular: - Fast runtime: Simple steps and quick computations. - Parallelizable: Can utilize multiple CPU cores or processors. - Easy to implement: Straightforward to understand and code, with minimal parameter tuning.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• Known K value: The number of clusters \( K \) is specified in advance.
  • Continuous features: Each data point can be represented as a vector of continuous values.

Example: In an archaeology survey, the location of an artifact might be expressed as:

\[ \mathbf{x} = [\text{east\_distance\_m}, \ \text{north\_distance\_m}] \]

For example, point \(X_3\) can be represented as:

\[ X_3 = [1.5, \ 4.2] \]

docs.title: Squared Euclidean Distance
docs.text:
For vectors \(\mathbf{X} = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)\) and \(\mathbf{Y} = (y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n)\):

\[ d^{2} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - y_i)^{2} \]

In K-Means, using Squared Euclidean Distance produces the same clustering result as Euclidean distance but is computationally more convenient.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Output of K-Means
docs.text:
• Cluster Assignments: Each data point belongs to exactly one cluster.
  • Cluster Centers: For each cluster \(k\), we find a centroid \(\mu_k\).

Example: If \(S_3\) is the set of data points assigned to the cluster with center \(\mu_3\), then:

\[ S_3 = \{\, \mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x} \ \text{is closest to} \ \mu_3 \,\} \]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Points to Note
docs.text:
• K-Means assumes continuous numeric features — categorical “Yes/No” data is not ideal.
  • Requires exact K value beforehand (which is not always known).
  • Not suited for purely binary vectors unless transformed appropriately.

↩ Back to Top| ⇧ Go to Top of This Topic

K-Means is a subset of general clustering problems in which: - Each data point is represented as a vector of continuous values. - Squared Euclidean Distance is used as the dissimilarity measure.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
The output of K-Means consists of:

  • A set of cluster centers: \( \mu_1, \mu_2, \dots, \mu_k \)
  • A set of assignments of data points to clusters:

\[ S_k = { \mathbf{x} \ | \ \mathbf{x} \ \text{is closest to} \ \mu_k } \]

The main goal: Minimize the Global Dissimilarity within clusters.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Global Dissimilarity
docs.text:
• Dissimilarity within a cluster = Sum of squared distances from each point to its cluster center:

\[ \text{ClusterDissimilarity}(S_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in S_k} | \mathbf{x} - \mu_k |^2 \]

  • Global Dissimilarity = Sum over all clusters:

\[ \text{GlobalDissimilarity} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in S_k} | \mathbf{x} - \mu_k |^2 \]

  • Objective Function: Minimize this global dissimilarity.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: The K-Means Algorithm (Lloyd’s Algorithm)
docs.text:
Steps:

  1. Initialize cluster centers
  2. Randomly pick \( K \) points from data (Random Initialization)

  3. Or use K-Means++ for better spread.

  4. Repeat until convergence:

  5. Assignment step: Assign each point to the cluster with the closest center:

    \[ \text{Assign}(\mathbf{x}) = \underset{k}{\mathrm{argmin}} \ | \mathbf{x} - \mu_k | \]

  6. Update step: Recalculate each cluster center as the mean of assigned points:

    \[ \mu_k = \frac{1}{|S_k|} \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in S_k} \mathbf{x} \]

docs.title: Notes on Efficiency
docs.text:
• Distance computation for each data point is independent → supports Embarrassingly Parallel Computation.
  • Algorithm always converges in finite time (though not necessarily to the global optimum).

docs.title: Key Considerations
docs.text:
• K must be known in advance (or determined with methods like the Elbow Method).
  • Works best with continuous numerical features.
  • Sensitive to initialization — K-Means++ helps.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Evaluation in Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning
docs.text:
In supervised learning (classification): - We have labeled data. - We split data into training data (with labels) and test data (with labels set aside for evaluation). - The evaluation is straightforward: Predict labels for the test data, compare with true labels, and compute the percentage of correct predictions.

In clustering (unsupervised): - We typically do not have labels. - If we do have access to a ground truth clustering (e.g., in archaeology or manually clustered images), we can compare results. - However, label permutations don’t affect correctness — what matters is whether pairs of points are in the same or different clusters in both our algorithm and the ground truth.

docs.title: External Evaluation Measures
docs.text:
When ground truth is available, we can use metrics like: - Rand Index - Adjusted Rand Index

These work by counting: - Pairs of data points that are in the same cluster in both algorithm and ground truth. - Pairs that are in different clusters in both.

Then they normalize the result for comparison.

docs.title: Challenges
docs.text:
• Rarely do we have ground truth in real clustering tasks.
  • Objective function values (like K-Means’ within-cluster sum of squares) let us compare different runs but do not tell us if the clustering is objectively “good.”
  • Evaluation may fail to capture the exact patterns we are looking for.

docs.title: 1. Visualization
docs.text:
• Plot the clustering results and visually inspect patterns.
  • Examples:
  • Archaeology clusters (clear groupings by location).
  • Image segmentation (distinguish objects).
  • Topic modeling (group related words and check coherence).

docs.title: 2. High-Dimensional Visualization Tools
docs.text:
• GGOBI: Useful for finding meaningful 2D projections of high-dimensional datasets.
  • Helpful when the dataset has many features (e.g., health metrics) and is not easily plottable.

docs.title: 3. Crowdsourced Evaluation
docs.text:
• Use platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to get human feedback on cluster quality.
  • Can be expensive in time and money.

docs.title: Internal Evaluation Measures
docs.text:
Do not require ground truth. Goal: Ensure points in the same cluster are close together, and points in different clusters are far apart.

Examples: - Silhouette Coefficient: Measures how similar a point is to its own cluster compared to other clusters. - Split-sample validation: Split the dataset, cluster each half, and compare the resulting cluster assignments.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• External Evaluation: Needs ground truth (e.g., Rand Index, Adjusted Rand Index).
  • Internal Evaluation: No ground truth needed (e.g., Silhouette Coefficient).
  • Visualization & Tools: Help qualitative assessment.
  • Crowdsourcing: Adds human judgment at a cost.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In clustering, ground truth information refers to the true, known class labels or actual group memberships of data points. It is the reference standard used to evaluate how well a clustering algorithm performs.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: When we perform clustering, the algorithm groups data based on similarity or distance measures without using labels. However, if we already have the true labels (ground truth), we can compare them to the predicted clusters to measure accuracy.

docs.title: When Ground Truth is Available
docs.text:
• Synthetic datasets: When we generate data with known cluster assignments.
  • Benchmark datasets: Public datasets like Iris, MNIST, or CIFAR-10 have known labels.
  • Pre-labeled business data: E.g., customer segments determined by domain experts.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Evaluation Metrics Using Ground Truth
docs.text:
When ground truth labels are available, clustering performance can be evaluated using external evaluation metrics, such as:

  1. Rand Index (RI) Measures the percentage of correct decisions made by the clustering algorithm.
  2. Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) Corrects RI for chance grouping.
  3. Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) Measures the similarity between predicted clusters and ground truth labels based on information theory.
  4. Fowlkes–Mallows Index (FMI) Measures the geometric mean of precision and recall for clustering.
  5. Purity Measures the extent to which clusters contain only members of a single class.

docs.title: When Ground Truth is NOT Available
docs.text:
If ground truth is unknown, we must rely on internal evaluation metrics (e.g., Silhouette Score, Davies–Bouldin Index) that do not require labels.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Scenario: We have data about animals described by physical traits (weight, number of legs, type of covering). - Ground Truth: Actual species name (Dog, Cat, Bird, etc.). - Predicted Clusters: Grouping from K-Means algorithm.

Evaluation: We can calculate ARI or NMI to see how close the K-Means clusters match the true species categories.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
We already know about the clustering problem and the particular algorithm for coming up with the solution — K-Means (also known as Lloyd’s Algorithm).

Now the question is: What happens if the output of the K-Means algorithm is not what we expected or wanted?

This section discusses: - Troubleshooting K-Means - Ways to make K-Means clustering better

↩ Go to Top of This Topic | ↩ Back to Global Top

docs.title: Ensuring Best Output
docs.text:
• Finite possibilities: K-Means eventually stops because there are only a finite number of possible clusterings.
  • Progress condition: The algorithm moves to a new clustering only if it decreases the K-Means objective function.
  • Not always quick: Although K-Means is generally fast, on some datasets it may take longer.

↩ Go to Top of This Topic | ↩ Back to Global Top

docs.title: Speed-Up Techniques
docs.text:
In K-Means, we normally compute the distance from every data point to every cluster center.

However, Triangle Inequality can help avoid checking every center.

Idea: If a data point is clearly closer to one cluster center, far-away centers can be skipped in comparisons — improving efficiency.

↩ Go to Top of This Topic | ↩ Back to Global Top

docs.title: Local vs Global Optimum
docs.text:
• Local Optimum: The point where K-Means stops might not be the minimum possible value of the objective function.
  • Global Optimum: The true minimum global dissimilarity — hard to guarantee in practice.

↩ Go to Top of This Topic | ↩ Back to Global Top

docs.title: 1. Multiple Random Initializations
docs.text: Run K-Means multiple times with different random starting points, then select the result with the lowest global dissimilarity. - Can be parallelized to reduce runtime impact.

docs.title: 2. Smarter Initialization — K-Means++
docs.text:
Improves centroid initialization by: - Starting with one random centroid. - Selecting subsequent centroids with probability proportional to the squared distance from the nearest existing centroid. - Ensures centroids are well spread apart. - Often improves both accuracy and runtime.

↩ Go to Top of This Topic | ↩ Back to Global Top

docs.title: Final Note
docs.text:
Even if we somehow reached the global optimum, we might still be dissatisfied with the results.

In that case, the problem might not be with the algorithm but with the clustering problem definition itself — a topic for later discussion.

↩ Go to Top of This Topic | ↩ Back to Global Top

As we know, Clustering is basically grouping data according to similarity. In this section, we explore different notions of grouping.

One immediate and obvious issue with K-Means clustering in various applications is that it requires the user to specify the number of clusters \(K\).

docs.title: Example: Image Segmentation
docs.text:
• Each data point = RGB values (pixel intensities).
  • K-Means finds \(K\) representative colors to approximate the full range of image colors.
  • K selection here is tied to the desired compression level.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
K-Means clustering is powerful, but it isn’t ideal for every dataset. It assumes Euclidean distance, spherical clusters, and similar cluster sizes. Sometimes we need different similarity notions.

↩ Back to This Topic’s Top · ↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Clusters of Unequal Size
docs.text:
• Issue: Large vs small clusters can be split incorrectly by K-Means.
  • Remedy: Use Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) with different covariances (fit via EM) to model unequal-sized/elliptical clusters.

↩ Back to This Topic’s Top · ↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Sensitivity to Outliers
docs.text:
• Issue: Euclidean distance is sensitive to extreme points, causing spurious clusters.
  • Remedy: Prefer robust distances or K-Medoids; consider trimming/outlier handling.

↩ Back to This Topic’s Top · ↩ Back to Top

docs.title: \(L_2\) (Euclidean)
docs.text: \[ d_{L2}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - y_i)^2} \]

docs.title: \(L_1\) (Manhattan)
docs.text:
\[ d_{L1}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert x_i - y_i \rvert \]
  • With \(L_1\), a K-Means–like procedure becomes K-Medoids (centers are medoids; in 1D the medoid is the median).

↩ Back to This Topic’s Top · ↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Clusters of Different Shapes
docs.text:

• Beyond K-Means: Data and Preprocessing
  • Is our data featurized?
  • Are features continuous numbers?
  • Are features commensurate (on-comparable-scales)
  • Too many features?
  • ↩ Back to Top

We have discussed different ways of troubleshooting the K-Means algorithm.

Now we will take a closer look at our data. In the archaeology example we discussed earlier, our dataset represented the locations of archaeological artifacts. For each data point, we recorded: - Distance east from a reference marker. - Distance north from the same marker.

However, datasets can take many other forms. Before running K-Means, we should ask the following questions:

docs.title: 1. Is Our Data Featurized?
docs.text:
Example: Suppose we have made a fitness app and collected data about our users such as: - Age - Height - Education - Post frequency on the app forum

K-Means requires a vector representation. Each entry in the vector is a feature with a particular meaning.

We can represent the dataset as a matrix where each row is a user, and each column is a feature.

docs.title: 2. Are Features Continuous Numbers?
docs.text: K-Means requires continuous-valued features. In the example: - Age: Already continuous (years). - Height: Convert to inches. - Education: Convert to years (e.g., 16 for a Bachelor's Degree). - Smoothie quantity: Keep as is.

docs.title: 3. Are Features Commensurate?
docs.text:
K-Means assumes spherical clusters (same width in all directions). If feature scales differ greatly (e.g., \(x \in [0,1]\), \(y \in [0,10]\)), the algorithm may produce skewed clusters.

Solution: - Normalization: Scale each feature to \([-1,1]\). - Standardization: Scale each feature to have a standard deviation of 1.

docs.title: 4. Are There Too Many Features?
docs.text:
Some features may be irrelevant or redundant. - If identified via domain knowledge, remove them beforehand. - Otherwise, use dimensionality reduction algorithms such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

Example: Recording a one-dimensional motion (spring and ball) with 5 cameras gives 4 redundant features. PCA extracts the most relevant feature.

docs.title: 5. Can We Use Domain Knowledge?
docs.text:
• Remove unhelpful features before PCA or K-Means.
  • Transform features to better fit K-Means assumptions if necessary.
  • Use domain-specific knowledge to improve results.

Summary: Preprocessing ensures that the K-Means algorithm works with optimal input data, improving clustering quality. Example Table (Raw Data):

Person Age Height Education Oz Smoothie Person 1 45 5'7" BA 8.2 Person 2 32 6'0" MS 10.5 Person 3 28 5'5" PhD 9.1

Example Table (After Feature Processing):

Person Age (years) Height (inches) Education (Encoded) Oz Smoothie Person 1 45 67 1 8.2 Person 2 32 72 2 10.5 Person 3 28 65 3 9.1 ---

docs.title: Assumptions of K-Means Clustering - Part 1
docs.text:
We already examined some of the assumptions in K-Means clustering and discussed what to do if we want to cluster the data but our application or data do not quite fit those assumptions.

K-Means Clustering is just one particular type of fixed \( K \) clustering — meaning the value of \( K \) is fixed. Here we also assume the number of clusters is finite. Even if we don’t know the number of clusters in advance, we often still assume that the number of clusters in our data is some fixed and finite number.

↩ Back to Top ↩ Go to Assumptions of K-Means Clustering

docs.title: When This Assumption Fails
docs.text:
This assumption might not always be correct. In big data scenarios, our dataset might not be static — we could have Streaming Data where new data is continuously added.

Example: - Wikipedia Phenomenon: - English Wikipedia alone averages around 800 new articles/day. - Even if we have read many articles before, new topics are constantly emerging. - Suppose we have 100 Wikipedia articles — we could cluster them into topics. - With thousands or millions of articles, new topics keep appearing over time.

↩ Back to Top ↩ Go to Assumptions of K-Means Clustering

docs.title: Growing Number of Clusters with Data Size
docs.text:
As datasets grow, the number of clusters may also grow. This means the complexity of our model should be able to scale with dataset size.

Examples: 1. Biological discovery: - Humans have discovered species for centuries, yet every week new species are found. - New clusters (species categories) appear as more data (observations) are collected.

  1. Fitness app data:

  2. Asking users about exercise routines will keep revealing new and unusual exercises, even after surveying thousands of people.

  3. Genetics and health:

  4. Studying more individuals’ DNA might reveal new, previously unknown ancestral populations.

  5. Observing more newborns could uncover new and unique health issues, prompting new treatment approaches.

  6. Social networks:

  7. As more people join, new friend groups and interests emerge over time.

↩ Back to Top ↩ Go to Assumptions of K-Means Clustering

docs.title: Moving Beyond Fixed \( K \)
docs.text:
In all these scenarios, we do not want a fixed \( K \) for clustering. Instead, we want \( K \) to grow with the size of the data.

↩ Back to Top ↩ Go to Assumptions of K-Means Clustering

docs.title: Non-Parametric Bayesian Methods
docs.text:
One solution is Non-Parametric Bayesian Methods: - Non-Parametric here means allowing many (potentially infinite) parameters. - The number of parameters grows as the dataset grows. - More complex than K-Means, but can adapt to dynamic datasets.

Recent advancement: - MAD-BAYES — Converts Non-Parametric Bayesian approaches into K-Means-like problems for clustering and other Unsupervised Learning tasks.

↩ Back to Top ↩ Go to Assumptions of K-Means Clustering

docs.title: Assumptions of K-Means Clustering - Part 2
docs.text:
In the last article, we discussed the case where we cannot assume a fixed number of clusters and where model complexity should grow with the size of the dataset.

In this article, we address cases where clustering does not adequately represent the hidden patterns we want to uncover in the data.

docs.title: When Clustering Fails to Capture Patterns
docs.text:
Example: - Suppose we have a website where people post pictures of their pets. - Ideally, we want a clustering algorithm to group: - All cat images into one cluster - All dog images into another - All lizard images into another

We could represent this clustering in a table/matrix: - Each row = one image - Each column = a cluster - A "1" in the corresponding column marks the image’s assigned cluster

Problem: - If someone posts a picture containing both a cat and a dog, which cluster does it belong to? - What if an image contains no animals?

K-Means forces each data point to belong to exactly one cluster. There may be uncertainty in assignment, but the underlying assumption is that there is one true group for each data point.

↩ Back to Top ↩ Go to Assumptions of K-Means Clustering

docs.title: Feature Allocation and Mixed Membership
docs.text:
In some cases, data points: - May belong to multiple groups simultaneously - May belong to no groups - May belong to only one group

Here, we call the groups features (different from earlier feature definitions) and the structure is a Feature Allocation instead of clustering.

Mixed Membership: - Data points can belong to multiple groups at once. - Clustering (or Mixture Models) assumes one group per data point. - Admixture Models allow multiple memberships per data point.

These terms — Feature Allocation, Mixed Membership, Admixture — all describe cases where items can belong to multiple groups.

↩ Back to Top ↩ Go to Assumptions of K-Means Clustering

docs.title: Applications of Mixed Membership Models
docs.text:
Text Analysis Example: - Analyzing New York Times archives may yield topics like sports, arts, and economics. - A movie review of Moneyball: - Arts → because it’s a movie review - Sports → because it’s about baseball - Economics → because it involves analytics/statistics in player trades

Genomics Example: - DNA may contain parts from multiple ancestral groups.

Social Networks Example: - One person may have work, family, and separate social identities.

↩ Back to Top ↩ Go to Assumptions of K-Means Clustering

docs.title: Algorithms Beyond Clustering
docs.text:
• Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA):
  • Originally for text data

  • Widely used for categorical datasets, including genetics

  • Feature Allocation with MAD-BAYES:

  • DP-Means and BP-Means algorithms used for tumor heterogeneity
  • Many tumors have multiple cancer types → identifying all types is crucial for treatment

↩ Back to Top ↩ Go to Assumptions of K-Means Clustering

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
In the previous module we learned about PCA, and how it can be applied to get patterns in the dataset and these patterns can capture more than 1 feature in the dataset.

In the user rating and holiday destination example we saw ratings for different holiday destinations can go up and down, i.e. they co-vary together or they have a high covariance, governed by some latent factors, for example, adventure.

Latent factors here mean hidden patterns that are inherent in the dataset but there is no feature for it and we can find this pattern using some technique, here we used PCA.

So, the goal of the PCA is to find the direction where the features co-vary the most together. This can be easily found using eigenvectors.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Computing Mean Ratings
docs.text:
To find this, we first take the dataset and build the covariance matrix for it.

To compute the covariance matrix we first compute the mean rating for each destination, as shown in the image below:

Person Alpine Spa Himalayas Hawaii Scuba Anne 20 4 16 0 Bill 10 2 18 10 Chris 13 1 19 7 Jen 1 13 7 19 Joe 18 10 10 2 Maggie 4 20 0 16 Average Rating 11 8.3 11.7 9

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Finding Deviations
docs.text:
The next step is to find the deviation for each person rating from the mean, and the covariance between the 2 destinations, say Himalayas and Hawaii, is the product of the deviation for both the destinations.

Formula: 

DEVIATION = (RATING OF PERSON i FOR LOCATION j) - (MEAN-RATING FOR LOCATION j)

Anne's Deviations: - Alpine Spa: 20 - 11 = 9 - Hawaii: 4 - 8.3 = -4.3 - Himalayas: 26 - 11.7 = 4.3 - Scuba: 0 - 9 = -9

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Covariance Calculation
docs.text:
To find the covariance between 2 destinations, we do the above settings for each person, that is find how much the person's rating deviates from the mean rating and multiply them. For example, the multiplication of Anne's deviation for the Himalayas and Hawaii is -18.49.

The covariance between, say, Himalayas and Hawaii is the sum of all the multiplications.

The covariance matrix is shown below:

                Alpine    Hawaii    Himalayas    Scuba
Alpine           56.8     -32.8      32.8      -56.8
Hawaii          -32.8      54.7     -54.7       32.8
Himalayas        32.8     -54.7      54.7      -32.8
Scuba           -56.8      32.8     -32.8       56.8

Note: If we have an n feature vector, this is an nn matrix, stating the covariance between any 2 combinations of destinations. For eg: the Himalayas are negatively correlated with Hawaii. In practicality, you don't have to do any of these calculations, Python did this for us*. Moreover, this is similar to what we have done in the FDS course, where we build a correlation matrix for different variables in python.

Now, the principal components we are looking for are the eigenvectors for this covariance matrix.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: What are eigenvectors?
docs.text:
We can defined it in terms of matrix and vectors, when we multiply a DxD matrix, here 3x3, with a Dx1 vector, here 3x1, and the result is another vector.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Matrix-Vector Multiplication
docs.text:
In the below example: - 11 = 61 + 21 + 31 - 3 = 21 + 01 + 11 - 6 = 31 + 11 + 2*1

MATRIX    VECTOR    RESULT
[6 2 3]     [1]       [11]
[2 0 1]  ×  [1]   =   [3]
[3 1 2]     [1]       [6]

Visual Representation: 

Original Vector (Blue):     →
Resultant Vector (Red):        ↗

Now, when we multiply the matrix with a vector, you get another vector, the direction and the magnitude of the resultant vector (11, 3, 6) are different from the original vector (1, 1, 1).

In the above example, the Blue vector is the original one, while the red vector is the resultant vector. The direction and magnitude of the resultant vector are different from the original.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: What Makes Eigenvectors Special
docs.text:
But, if the original vector is an eigenvector, we can only see the magnitude change, and the direction does not change.

Here, the vector (0.85, 0.26, 0.45) is an eigenvector, and 8.2 is the corresponding eigenvalue, as the resulting vector is the same as the original vector, only the magnitude of the resultant vector is 8.2x.

MATRIX    EIGENVECTOR    EIGENVALUE × EIGENVECTOR
[6 2 3]      [.85]              [.85]
[2 0 1]  ×   [.26]   =   8.2 ×  [.26]
[3 1 2]      [.45]              [.45]

Visual Representation: 

Original Eigenvector (Blue):     →
Resultant Vector (Red):          ──→  (same direction, 8.2x longer)

In some sense, eigenvectors capture the major direction that is inherent in the matrix, and the larger the eigenvalue, the more important the vector.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Mathematical Definition
docs.text:
The above can be written as the equation as shown below:

A × x = λ × x

Where: - A = MATRIX - x = EIGENVECTOR - λ = EIGENVALUE

We don't have to worry about this equation, the computer will solve this for us in split seconds.

Another point to note here is that, if we have a DxD matrix, then we will have D eigenvectors and eigenvalues. The highest eigenvalue will have a corresponding eigenvector that captures the major direction in the matrix.

Now, we learned at the start of the video, that the goal of the PCA is to find the direction where the features co-vary the most together and this can be done using eigenvectors.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Graph clustering is a fundamental technique in network analysis that helps identify communities or groups within complex networks. Unlike traditional clustering where data points have explicit features, graph clustering relies solely on the connectivity patterns between nodes. This approach is essential for understanding the structure of social networks, biological systems, web pages, and many other real-world networks.

The main challenge in graph clustering is to identify dense groups of nodes (clusters) that are well-connected internally but have fewer connections to other clusters. This document explores various methods and criteria for achieving effective graph clustering.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Nodes and Edges
docs.text:
In graph theory, data points are represented as nodes (also called vertices), and the relationships between them are represented as edges. This is fundamentally different from traditional data analysis where each data point has a set of features.

Key Components: - Node: Represents a data point in the graph - Edge: Represents a connection or relationship between two nodes

docs.title: Edge Weights
docs.text: Edges can have weights associated with them, where: - Larger weight = Stronger relationship between nodes - Smaller weight = Weaker relationship between nodes

docs.title: Network Examples
docs.text:
Common types of networks include: - Social Media Networks: Users connected by friendships or interactions - Web Page Networks: Pages connected by hyperlinks - Biological Networks: Proteins connected by interactions - Transportation Networks: Cities connected by routes

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: What is a Cluster?
docs.text: A cluster in a graph is an intuitive concept that consists of nodes that are well-connected with each other. The formal definition involves nodes that have many edges between them, creating a dense subgraph.

docs.title: Volume and Density
docs.text:
Volume: The number of edges within a cluster Density: Volume per node, which indicates how tightly connected the cluster is

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: First Criterion: High Density
docs.text: For a good cluster, we want the density (volume per node) to be large. This ensures that nodes within a cluster are well-connected to each other.

docs.title: Second Criterion: Low Inter-cluster Connections
docs.text: There should be fewer edges between different clusters, ensuring good separation between distinct groups.

docs.title: Cut Value
docs.text:
The Cut Value is defined as the number of edges that need to be removed to separate a cluster from the rest of the graph.

Formula: Cut(C) = number of edges between cluster C and the rest of the graph

docs.title: Problems with Simple Cut Value
docs.text:
Using only the cut value as a criterion can be problematic. For example, an outlier node connected by a single edge would have a cut value of 1, but it doesn't represent a meaningful cluster.

Key Issue: Cut value alone doesn't consider the size of the cluster, leading to poor clustering results.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Conductance
docs.text:
Conductance balances the cut value with the cluster size by dividing the cut by a measure of volume.

Formula: 

Conductance(C) = Cut(C) / min{Volume(C), Volume(V\C)}

docs.title: Normalized Cut
docs.text:
Normalized cut is another metric that balances separation and cluster size.

Formula: 

Ncut(C) = Cut(C) / [Volume(C) + Volume(V\C)]

docs.title: Formula Analysis
docs.text:
In both formulas: - Small volume → Small denominator → Large criterion value - Large volume → Large denominator → Small criterion value

Optimization Goal: Minimize these criteria to find good clusters

Characteristics of Good Clusters: - Not too small - Internally well-connected - Well separated from other nodes

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Matrix Definition
docs.text:
An adjacency matrix is an N×N matrix where N is the number of nodes in the graph.

Matrix Values: - 1 if there is an edge between two nodes - 0 if there is no edge between two nodes

docs.title: Block Structure
docs.text:
When nodes are arranged by their cluster membership, the adjacency matrix shows a clear block-like structure:

Cluster Node 1 Node 2 Node 3 Node 4 Node 5 1-1 0 1 0 1 1 1-2 1 0 0 0 1 2-1 0 0 1 1 0 2-2 0 0 0 1 0

docs.title: Shuffled Structure
docs.text:
In practice, node structure is usually shuffled arbitrarily, making clusters less obvious in the adjacency matrix. The clustering algorithms must identify these hidden patterns.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Modularity Clustering
docs.text:
Purpose: Measures how high the density of edges within clusters is compared to a baseline graph where edges occur randomly.

Key Features: - Compares actual cluster density to random baseline - Helps identify statistically significant communities - Useful for large networks where examining the entire network is impractical

docs.title: Correlation Clustering
docs.text:
Approach: Uses information about pairs of points to determine if they should be in the same cluster.

Method: - If two nodes are similar, they should be in the same cluster - Uses various similarity measures to quantify node relationships - Can incorporate different types of node features or connectivity patterns

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
Graph clustering has numerous real-world applications:

  1. Social Network Analysis
  2. Understanding how epidemics spread
  3. Analyzing how trends and opinions propagate

  4. Identifying influential users or communities

  5. Biological Networks

  6. Protein interaction analysis
  7. Understanding biological pathways

  8. Drug discovery and target identification

  9. Web Analysis

  10. Identifying related web pages
  11. Improving search algorithms

  12. Detecting web communities

  13. Transportation and Infrastructure

  14. Route optimization
  15. Network resilience analysis
  16. Traffic flow management

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Graph clustering is a powerful technique for understanding the structure of complex networks. The key insights include:

  1. Multiple Criteria Needed: Simple metrics like cut value alone are insufficient; balanced approaches like conductance and normalized cut provide better results.

  2. Trade-off Management: Good clustering requires balancing internal connectivity (high density) with external separation (low cut value).

  3. Scalability Considerations: For large networks, sampling and specialized algorithms like modularity clustering become essential.

  4. Application Diversity: The techniques apply across many domains, from social networks to biological systems.

  5. Matrix Visualization: Adjacency matrices provide a useful way to visualize cluster structure, though real-world data often requires sophisticated algorithms to reveal hidden patterns.

Understanding these principles enables effective analysis of network structures and extraction of meaningful insights from complex relational data.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Spectral clustering is a powerful graph-based clustering method that leverages the magic of eigenvectors to understand the global connectivity structure of graphs. Unlike traditional clustering methods, spectral clustering uses the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian matrix to encode structural information about the graph.

The key insight is that eigenvectors help us find inherent directions in datasets - similar to how PCA uses eigenvectors from covariance matrices to find major directions of variance, spectral clustering uses eigenvectors from the Laplacian matrix to understand graph structure and identify natural clusters.

Key Question Addressed: How do we compute similarity criteria for graph clustering when nodes don't have inherent feature vectors?

Answer: We use the spectral properties (eigenvalues and eigenvectors) of the graph Laplacian matrix to create meaningful embeddings and identify cluster structure.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Graph Laplacian Matrix
docs.text: The Laplacian matrix is the fundamental mathematical object in spectral clustering. It encodes the connectivity structure of a graph in a matrix format.

docs.title: Construction Rules:
docs.text:
• Off-diagonal elements: -1 if there's an edge between nodes i and j, 0 otherwise
  • Diagonal elements: The degree of each node (number of edges connected to that node)

docs.title: Example Graph and Laplacian:
docs.text:
Consider a graph with 6 nodes connected as shown in the original document:

Node 1 2 3 4 5 6 1 2 -1 -1 0 0 0 2 -1 2 -1 0 0 0 3 -1 -1 3 -1 0 0 4 0 0 -1 3 -1 -1 5 0 0 0 -1 2 -1 6 0 0 0 -1 -1 2

Node Degrees: - Node 1: degree = 2 (connected to nodes 2 and 3) - Node 2: degree = 2 (connected to nodes 1 and 3) - Node 3: degree = 3 (connected to nodes 1, 2, and 4) - And so on...

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
docs.text: From the Laplacian matrix, we compute eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors, sorted in ascending order of eigenvalues.

docs.title: Example Eigenvalue Decomposition:
docs.text:
Eigenvalues 0 0.4 3 3 3 4.6 Eigenvector Components Node 1 0.41 -0.46 -0.05 0.71 0.28 0.18 Node 2 0.41 -0.46 -0.05 -0.71 0.28 0.18 Node 3 0.41 -0.26 0.10 0.00 -0.57 -0.66 Node 4 0.41 0.26 0.10 0.00 -0.57 0.66 Node 5 0.41 0.46 -0.75 0.00 0.16 -0.18 Node 6 0.41 0.46 0.65 0.00 0.41 -0.18

Key Insights: - We focus on the smallest and largest eigenvalues - The smallest eigenvalue is always 0 for connected graphs - Each eigenvector has one entry per node, creating a feature representation

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Connected Components
docs.text: The number of zero eigenvalues directly corresponds to the number of connected components in the graph.

docs.title: Example: Graph with 3 Connected Components
docs.text:
• Eigenvalues: [0, 0, 0, 2, 3, 3]
  • Interpretation: Three zero eigenvalues → Three separate connected components
  • This provides immediate insight into graph structure without complex analysis

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Second Eigenvector Analysis
docs.text: The second smallest eigenvector (corresponding to the second smallest eigenvalue) reveals crucial structural information about the graph.

docs.title: Key Properties:
docs.text:
• Each node gets a value from the eigenvector
  • Closer nodes in the graph structure receive similar values
  • Values can be color-coded to visualize clustering patterns
  • Natural partitions emerge from the value distribution

docs.title: Color Coding Scheme:
docs.text:
• Blue: Lower values in the eigenvector
  • Red: Higher values in the eigenvector
  • Gradient: Intermediate values show smooth transitions

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Color Coding and Partitioning
docs.text:
When nodes are colored based on their eigenvector values:

  1. Structural similarity becomes visually apparent
  2. Natural partitions can be identified (shown as red dotted lines in visualizations)
  3. Cluster boundaries emerge from the eigenvector value distribution
  4. Connected regions tend to have similar colors

This approach works even when nodes have no inherent features - the structure itself provides the clustering information.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Feature Vector Assignment
docs.text: Since graph nodes typically don't have feature vectors, spectral clustering creates embeddings using eigenvector values.

docs.title: Embedding Process:
docs.text:
1. Extract values: Take one value from each eigenvector for each node
  2. Create feature vector: Combine these values into a multi-dimensional representation
  3. Result: Each node now has a feature vector derived from graph structure

docs.title: Comparison with PCA:
docs.text:
• PCA: Uses eigenvectors with largest eigenvalues for dimensionality reduction
  • Spectral Clustering: Uses eigenvectors with smallest eigenvalues for clustering

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 2D Coordinate Mapping
docs.text: Using the second and third smallest eigenvectors as coordinates creates a 2D embedding of the graph.

docs.title: Visualization Benefits:
docs.text:
• Spatial proximity: Connected nodes appear close in the 2D space
  • Cluster identification: Graph clusters become spatial clusters
  • Edge stretch minimization: Connected nodes are positioned to minimize edge length

docs.title: Coordinate Assignment:
docs.text:
Node_i_coordinates = (eigenvector_2[i], eigenvector_3[i])

This creates a natural 2D representation where graph structure is preserved spatially.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Small Eigenvalues - Minimizing Edge Stretch
docs.text: Eigenvectors corresponding to small eigenvalues have a specific optimization goal:

docs.title: Behavior:
docs.text:
• Minimize edge stretch: Connected nodes receive similar values
  • Preserve local structure: Nearby nodes cluster together in embedding space
  • Create cohesive clusters: Graph communities become tight spatial groups

docs.title: Mathematical Goal:
docs.text:
Minimize: ∑(edges) (value(i) - value(j))²

Where value(i) and value(j) are the eigenvector values for connected nodes i and j.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Large Eigenvalues - Maximizing Edge Stretch
docs.text: Eigenvectors corresponding to large eigenvalues behave oppositely:

docs.title: Behavior:
docs.text:
• Maximize edge stretch: Connected nodes receive very different values
  • Spread out structure: Connected nodes are placed far apart in embedding
  • Create dispersed layouts: No clear clustering patterns emerge

docs.title: Visual Result:
docs.text:
• Nodes appear scattered across the embedding space
  • Connected nodes are positioned far from each other
  • Clustering structure is destroyed

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Edge Distance Formula
docs.text:
The fundamental principle behind spectral clustering involves optimizing edge-based distances:

Total_Edge_Stretch = ∑(all edges (i,j)) (value(i) - value(j))²

Where: - value(i) = eigenvector value assigned to node i - value(j) = eigenvector value assigned to node j - The sum is over all edges in the graph

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Small Eigenvalue Eigenvectors:
docs.text:
• Objective: Minimize total edge stretch
  • Result: Similar values for connected nodes
  • Use case: Clustering and community detection

docs.title: Large Eigenvalue Eigenvectors:
docs.text:
• Objective: Maximize total edge stretch
  • Result: Different values for connected nodes
  • Use case: Maximum separation and dispersion

docs.title: Why This Works:
docs.text:
1. Graph structure constraint: Eigenvectors must satisfy Laplacian properties
  2. Optimization pressure: Eigenvalue magnitude determines stretch minimization/maximization
  3. Natural clustering: Small eigenvalues automatically group structurally similar nodes

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Key Insights from Spectral Clustering
docs.text:
1. Structural Information: Eigenvectors encode rich information about graph connectivity
  2. Automatic Feature Creation: No need for predefined node features
  3. Natural Partitioning: Cluster boundaries emerge from the mathematical structure
  4. Scalable Approach: Works with the graph Laplacian regardless of graph size

docs.title: Practical Applications
docs.text:
• Social Network Analysis: Finding communities and groups
  • Image Segmentation: Treating pixels as graph nodes
  • Biological Networks: Identifying functional modules
  • Recommendation Systems: Clustering users or items based on interaction graphs

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Spectral clustering demonstrates the "magic of eigenvectors" by: - Transforming structural graph information into numerical embeddings - Automatically identifying natural cluster boundaries - Providing both local and global graph structure insights - Creating meaningful representations from pure connectivity information

The method's power lies in its ability to extract clustering information directly from graph structure, making it invaluable for analyzing complex networks where traditional feature-based approaches fall short.

↩ Back to Top
